caption:
Bryan Johnson turned his body into a lab and proved health can be measured and managed like a project. Everything we learned from it is about a male body.

There's no female version. No open protocol that accounts for cycles, hormones, menopause and real female biochemistry. Lots of advice — almost no data.

So I'm building SOMA: running a longevity protocol in public, with labs and numbers, and showing what works for a woman's body and what doesn't.

Follow for baseline labs next week.

#longevity #womenshealth #healthspan

slides.bg: a single empty examination chair in a dark clinical room, sensor cables and electrode pads coiled on the seat, one cold blue light source from the left and a faint warm lamp on the right, deep shadow, still-life photograph, the room is empty, nobody is present, no person, no face, no hands
slides.text:
Bryan Johnson spends about
$2M a year to *not age*

Nobody's doing it for women

slides.bg: A still-life product photograph, shot straight down onto a white table from directly above. On the table: two weekly pill organisers filled with capsules, a blood collection tube with a purple cap, a smartwatch lying flat, and a neat stack of printed lab report pages. Bright even studio light. Nothing else is in the frame — no person, no face, no eyes, no hands, no body, no reflection of a person. Objects only.
slides.text:
30 doctors.
100+ pills a day.
Every organ measured.

All on *one body* — a man's

slides.bg: a black and white archival photograph of a 1970s clinical research ward, a row of empty hospital beds and a metal equipment trolley, grainy film, high contrast, documentary style, the room is empty, nobody is present, no people
slides.text:
Until *1993* women were mostly
left out of clinical trials in the US

The cycle "messed up the data"

slides.bg: a close overhead photograph of a printed laboratory results sheet on a desk, columns of numbers and a reference range column, a pen resting beside it, soft daylight from a window, shallow depth of field, still-life photograph, no people, no hands
slides.text:
So most protocols, doses and
"normal ranges" are still built for men

Your cycle, iron, thyroid,
perimenopause — usually
*not even in the spreadsheet*

slides.bg: a woman seen from behind in silhouette standing in a dark room facing a wall of blank glowing screens, only her shoulders and hair visible against the light, cinematic, one light source, moody, her face is not visible
slides.text:
There is no *female Bryan Johnson*

Doctors write about women's health.
Influencers sell supplements.

Nobody is running a full protocol
out loud — with real numbers

slides.bg: A flat graphic artwork on a pale cream paper ground: three smooth curved lines rising and falling across the frame, two in muted grey and one in warm terracotta, with four faint vertical bands behind them dividing the width into quarters. Printed editorial texture. Abstract shapes only — no text, no numbers, no labels, no people, no face, no silhouette, no shadow of a person.
slides.text:
Imagine data like this

How biomarkers shift across a cycle.
What actually works in perimenopause.
Which tests to take, and how to read
them as a woman.
